definition: Plaintive means sounding sad or mournful, especially describing a sound, voice, or cry.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word plaintive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know plaintive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The loon's plaintive call carried across the misty lake long after sunset.
Wistful is weaker than plaintive: a wistful tone carries gentle longing, while a plaintive one is openly sad and mournful.
Anguished is stronger than plaintive — an anguished cry expresses raw, unbearable pain, while a plaintive one is sorrowful without that intensity.

Mournful means full of sorrow or grief, as if grieving an actual loss — mournful faces, a mournful procession, black crepe on the door. Plaintive lives in sound and asks less: a plaintive cry or melody simply sounds sad and appealing, with no real bereavement required behind it.

Sorrowful means expressing sadness, and it can describe almost anything — eyes, news, a whole chapter. Plaintive is the sound-specific cousin: a thin, sad, touching quality in a voice, cry, or tune. Sorrowful states the emotion; plaintive is how that emotion reaches the ear.

The violinist set up at the far end of the subway platform on Friday evenings, where the tile curved and the sound could bloom.
Most weeks she played reels and show tunes, quick bright things for the commuter rush.
But when the last express pulled away she would end with an old air, and the melody turned plaintive — thin, sad, and strangely appealing as it drifted down the empty platform.
A transit worker once asked if the tune had been written for a funeral.
She laughed and said no; nothing sad had ever happened to it, or to her.
The sorrow lived in the sound itself, she explained — in the slides and the minor turns — and that was exactly why strangers stopped to listen.
